skyline.text: How the means of production landed on Amit Varma’s laptop
Ajay Shah on the failures that military secrecy hides
Johan Norberg on the free markets behind Nordic welfare states

footnote.text: There’s a paid version, but not necessary.

brief.head: Weak and too busy
brief.text: Amit Varma recalled Francis Fukuyama’s two axes, scope and strength. The ideal is a strong state with limited scope; India, he said, has a weak state that does too much. {026-C02}

brief.head: Words in disguise
brief.text: Economics repurposes plain English words such as market failure, public good and moral hazard, Ajay Shah said. They seem “seductively accessible”, but each is a technical term. {026-C06}

brief.head: Knowledge is hard
brief.text: Utilitarian thinkers assume knowledge is easy, Amit Varma said. Anyone who claims freedom isn’t working should face “a really high bar of proof”. {026-C07}

brief.head: Even if you don’t care
brief.text: Suppose you value order or tradition, not liberty, Ajay Shah said. Even then, a baseline of freedom and a state confined to market failure is the path to prosperity. {026-C08}

brief.head: Four-word mantra
brief.text: Amit Varma’s question for any problem in society is “Where is the coercion?” Find the coercion, he said, and you find the root of the problem. {026-C10}

thought.text: We must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.
thought.who: Amit Varma, quoting *Yes Minister*, or was it *Yes Prime Minister*, on the urge to act

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the limits of the state
lead.head: Freedom first, state on probation
body: Leave people alone by default. Let the state in only where it can make some people better off without hurting anybody, and only where it can actually succeed.
That was the toolkit Amit Varma and Ajay Shah built in this episode, picking up from their last one on the state.

The state is always coercive, Varma recalled, and it pays for everything with taxes it takes by force. So every proposal that it act must be justified. “Each time we are justifying violence,” he said. {026-C01}
The hard part is drawing the lines without it becoming, in Shah’s words, “your philosophy versus mine”.
## A lunch that is free

Economists, Shah said, have built a framework for this. Freedom is the baseline. Then there is a narrow class of problems, called market failure, where “the correct kind of state intervention is a free lunch because it will make some people in society better off without harming anybody at all”. {026-C03}
That makes it common ground. “We’re not doing Robin Hood,” Shah said. It is not about taking from the rich, and it does not ignite class warfare.
Market failures come in four buckets: market power, externalities, asymmetric information and public goods. Outside them, freedom stays the default.
## Hold it there
Spotting a market failure only starts the conversation. “Do not rush in where angels fear to tread,” Shah said. {#angels}
Very many times, he said, the state marches into something and it becomes a mess. So before intervening, ask how hard the job will be.
For that he offered a test simple enough for a conversation over chai. Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock posed two questions in a 2004 paper; Shah and Vijay Kelkar added two more.
Are there many transactions? Do frontline staff have discretion? Are the stakes high? Is there secrecy? Four yes-or-no answers tell you whether a problem is easy or hard. {026-C12}
A polio drive is easy: many transactions, but no discretion. Criminal justice is hard: the accused faces jail, and “the dangers of corruption and discretion just go to infinity”.

Among the ways to fix a problem, Shah said, pick the least intrusive, and go to the root cause: when the air is bad, “don’t build hospitals”. Each problem, too, belongs at the lowest level of government that can take it.
And sometimes the answer is to walk away. A bad intervention, Shah said, can be worse than living with the market failure it claims to fix.
## A slow apprenticeship
No state learns all this overnight. Europe’s states, Shah said, spent centuries mostly raising taxes and waging war, and learned in the process how to be a state.
India, he argued, should start with a very low scope, the police and the judiciary, and for one or two generations learn how to do those few things. {026-C16}
Arguing over more welfare or less, he said, is not useful while such basic problems burn.

Varma, citing the writer Johan Norberg, said the Nordic countries got rich as free-market economies before they built welfare states. Copy one Swedish outcome, Shah warned, and you need Swedish rule of law behind it.
“It’s not an NGO, it’s not a nice guy, it’s not a mother,” Shah said of the state. “It’s a coercive creature with its own self-interest.”

second.label: Public goods
second.head: Clean air, by drone
second.deck: Ajay Shah on what a public good really is, and what it isn’t
body: A public good is not anything that happens to be good for the public, Ajay Shah said. Technically, it is non-rival and non-excludable. {026-C05}

One young woman walking safely down a street does not use up its safety, and no one could, even in theory, exclude a newborn child from breathing clean air. So the pollution over North India is a true public-goods problem.

Shah would back taxes to put 10,000 drones over the Hindi heartland, find every fire and ticket whoever lit it. {#drones} India’s so-called digital public goods, by contrast, are generally rival and excludable, he said.

quote.text: The welfareist socialist impulse in India is anything that is good for the people is a public good, and that’s just wrong.

second.caption: the public good of clean air

third.head: Friendly to whom?
body: People assume that business-friendly means market-friendly, Amit Varma said. “They’re absolutely the opposite.” {026-C09}

Market-friendly means competition and free entry, which serves consumers. Business-friendly means looking after the businesses already there, which want to keep competitors out. Every big business wants to be a monopoly, he said, and lobbies the government for tariffs and regulations.

Genuine monopolies, Varma argued, are incredibly rare in a competitive marketplace. Look closely at one and you usually find cronyism, or a state that has blocked entry in some way. Or it is not a monopoly at all, and someone has defined it wrongly.
Ajay Shah, for his part, warned against the populist urge to punish monopolists out of envy. A natural monopoly, he said, may need only its prices regulated, not to be broken up. {#natural}
third.caption: business-friendly and market-friendly

p2.title: Rules of engagement
p2.deck: Market failure, four hard questions and a good deal of patience: when, the hosts asked, should the state act?

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Some better off, none worse
sections.caption: market failure and its four buckets
body: Amit Varma first recalled where the hosts stood: the state is always coercive, and India “happens to have a weak state that does too much”. {026-C02}
Ajay Shah took it from there. Freedom is the baseline: human beings, he said, “should swing their arms wildly and not be constrained by a boom arm required by a government regulator”.

Then there is a narrow class of problems, called market failure, where the right intervention makes some people better off without harming anybody. That, Shah argued, is a technical core everyone can agree on, with no Robin Hood and no class warfare. {026-C03}
## Four buckets
The first bucket is market power. Even a monopoly, he said, should be handled in ways the monopolist could sign on to, not out of envy and resentment.

The second is externalities, spillovers nobody contracted for. If I get vaccinated, you are better off, so I underinvest; if I play loudspeakers, I destroy your peace. “My freedom to move my fist should be limited not just by the absence of the boom arm, but by the proximity of your nose.”
The third is asymmetric information: grandmothers and dentists cannot tell whether a bank is sound. Google gutter oil, Shah urged: “It will blow your mind.” {026-J05}
~ The fourth is public goods, such as clean air. Outside these four, freedom stays the default. “These are green lighted by the economists as market failure,” Shah said. {026-C04}

quote.text: It’s very important to note we’re not doing populism. We’re not taking money from the rich and giving it to the poor.

sections.label: The caveats
sections.head: Where is the coercion?
sections.caption: the high bar of proof
body: Amit Varma agreed with the framework entirely, then added his warnings. To say that freedom “doesn’t quite work” somewhere is a utilitarian claim about consequences, he said.

“One of my issues with all utilitarian thinking is that it assumes that knowledge is easy,” he said. “Knowledge is not easy.” Thinkers with an engineering mindset predict that if we do this, that will happen, and none of it happens. {026-C07}
People cite market failure to justify state intervention, he added, but no one talks of state failure, which public choice theory shows to be practically ubiquitous.
## Plain words, fine print

Language muddies things too. Not finding a green cushion in a shop of blue ones, Varma said, is no market failure. Ajay Shah called it the bane of his field that economics repurposes plain English words, unlike science and mathematics. {026-C06}
Varma’s own test is four words long. Faced with any problem in society, he asks: “Where is the coercion?” In his case, he said, that is always where the root lies. {026-C10}
~ Even an apparent monopoly, he argued, usually turns out to be defined wrongly or propped up by the state.

quote.text: The bar of proof should be very high. It should not be something that you can use conveniently to crush freedom

sections.label: The difficulty test
sections.head: Four questions over chai
sections.caption: how hard an intervention will be
body: “Just because there’s a market failure, it doesn’t mean that a state intervention will succeed,” Ajay Shah said. So before acting, ask how hard the battle will be.

He wanted a test simple enough for every drawing room in the country, one the “great dictator Amit Bhai” could apply over chai. The first two questions come from a 2004 paper by Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock. {026-R07}
Are there many transactions? Do frontline staff have discretion? Shah and Vijay Kelkar added two: are the stakes high, and is there secrecy?
## Easy drops, hard cases
A polio drive has many transactions but no discretion. Staff walk into a slum or village, put the drop on everyone and follow a manual, so it rolls out easily.

A teacher who skips her government school steals ₹15,000 a month, so the effort put into misbehaviour is limited. {#teacher} But when the accused in a criminal case faces jail, the stakes are sky high, and so is the pull towards corruption.
Secrecy hides failure. The military is admired, Shah said, but its secrecy is likely cover for a lot of state failure. {026-S03}
~ Four yes-or-no answers, he said, tell you straight away whether you face an easy problem or a hard one. {026-C12}

quote.text: In these four zero one numbers, you’ve got a grip of the essence that some things are easy, some things are hard

sections.label: The lightest touch
sections.head: Knock, but don’t come in
sections.caption: the least intrusive intervention
body: If there are ten ways to intervene, choose the least oppressive, Amit Varma said, reminding Ajay Shah of a point from the book Shah wrote with Vijay Kelkar.

Shah agreed. “A good intervention is one that is the least intrusive in the lives of people,” he said. The liberal dream is to live on your own terms, without needing to think about the state at all. {026-C13}
He sketched some rules. Touching a human body is worse than not touching it; knocking on a door is worse than not knocking; entering a house is worse than standing at the door.
The cheapest fix, he added, is at the root cause: build good roads rather than a trauma centre at every highway exit.
## Closer to home

Varma argued for government that is as local as possible. Kerala’s problem is diabetes and obesity, Bihar’s is malnourishment, yet central schemes are designed in Delhi around the problems nearby. {026-S04}

Shah named the idea: the subsidiarity principle, which places every problem at the lowest level of government where it can be placed. {026-C14} He called it one of the great ideas in economics, prompting Varma to ask how many there were.
~ You don’t always have to do something, Varma said: government “has limited capacity, limited money, limited bandwidth”. {026-C15}

quote.text: Living with a market failure is often better than living with a bad state intervention that claims to address that market failure

sections.label: Learning by doing
sections.head: Sweden wasn’t built in a day
sections.caption: how states learn to be states
body: Did the immense scope of the Swedish state emerge pristine into the world? “Of course not,” Ajay Shah said. Nobody can build the Swedish state overnight.
In Europe in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, he said, states mostly raised taxes and waged war. “It took hundreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.” {026-S02}
So it is always wise to start with a very low scope, Shah argued, and spend one or two generations learning to do a few narrow things. {026-C16}

For India, he means basics like the police and the judiciary. “For 25 years, for 50 years, we have to learn how to do basics,” he said. {#basics} Only then should society debate widening the state’s scope.
## The Nordic question

Amit Varma took on the familiar retort about Scandinavia. Behind their welfare states, he said, the Nordic countries keep great individual liberty, and starting a business there is far easier than in India.
They also became rich before they became welfare states. The writer Johan Norberg, Varma said, shows that they were model free-market economies first. {026-R15}
~ Shah added that one Swedish result cannot be copied without the rest: “Swedish levels of the cashless economy is backed by Swedish levels of rule of law.” {026-C17}

quote.text: So it’s always wise to start with a very low scope, start with a few narrow problems

side.boxText: Market failure, the extended test of difficulty and the least intrusive intervention all come from *In Service of the Republic* by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah. Amit Varma calls it “a masterpiece available to you at your nearest bookstore”. {026-R03}

contQuote.text: As a card carrying economist, I’m saying to you that societies flourish when freedom is a baseline and government intervention is limited to the class of market failures where there can be a successful implementation.

p3.title: Tales of the state
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts told, from Bollywood’s colour grading to Russia’s army

stories.start: my favorite little story which I have said on the scene and the unseen
stories.end: could afford to own it and they would kind of rent it out
stories.caption: the $800,000 colour-grading software
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how the means of production got cheap
stories.head: Hollywood colour, laptop price
body: Ajay Shah opened the episode smiling. The clunky boom arms were gone, replaced by new wireless microphones from Rode that record audio in 32-bit float. “We’ve got a new level of human freedom,” Shah said. “We can wave our arms around.” {026-R19}
Amit Varma, who feared that one day he would disappear and Shah would be even happier, likened 32-bit float to RAW in photography: everything is captured, so the levels can be fixed later. {#raw}

Shah saw a German philosopher in all this: the proletariat owning the means of production. “You and I, humble slaves and producers, are no longer the subjects of the giant media companies,” he said. Varma had guessed Immanuel Kant; the exchange ended on a pun: “Now Immanuel can.” {026-J02}

Then Varma told his favourite story about the means of production. DaVinci Resolve is today one of the big three editing programs. Anyone can download it free, and the free version gives state-of-the-art editing and the best colour grading.
It was not always so. Back in 2010, when it did only colour grading, Varma asked Shah to guess the price. {#grading} Shah ventured that it was more than most Indian media companies would pay.
“There wasn’t one in India because it cost eight hundred thousand dollars for colour grading,” Varma said. {026-S01}
~ So Bollywood films were sent to Hollywood for colour grading and shipped back, with the rental part of the cost. Varma called the change “utterly miraculous”.
stories.why: In about a decade, a tool only a few studios could afford became free. The means of production now sit with individual creators, which is what lets two people make their own show.
stories.postscript: Shah’s shirt came from Indian Colours, which licenses Indian artists’ work and pays them royalties, much as authors earn on books.

stories.start: Did the immense scope of the Swedish state emerge pristine into the world?
stories.end: which could then be applied to new problems such as vaccines
stories.caption: how Europe learned to be a state
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how European states learned their trade
stories.head: Tax, fight, repeat
body: Sweden’s vast state did not spring up overnight, Ajay Shah said. In every advanced economy, learning to run a state correctly took hundreds of years. {026-C16}

In Europe in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, states did essentially two things. They ran a fiscal system to raise taxes, the so-called fiscus, and they waged war, with all the contracting and technology that arms required. {026-S02}

Doing those narrow jobs over and over, they learned HR, contracting, checks and balances and how to control corruption. They learned to solve principal-agent problems, and to keep the military in its barracks inside a liberal democracy.
~ Only then, Shah said, were those hard-won lessons applied to new problems, such as vaccines.

quote.text: It took hundreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.

stories.postscript: Shah’s prescription for India: 25 to 50 years of learning the basics, such as the police and the judiciary. {#basics}

stories.start: So another example which I got from episodes on centrally sponsored schemes
stories.end: they're calculated for solving the nearby problem and therefore not understanding local needs
stories.caption: Kerala’s diabetes and Bihar’s hunger
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Delhi’s schemes miss
stories.head: Kerala’s sugar, Bihar’s hunger
body: Amit Varma took his example from two of his own conversations: one with Pranay Kotasthane on centrally sponsored schemes, and one with RS Nilakantan about his book on South India. {026-S04}
The needs of the North and the South, he said, are very different. Kerala has a problem of diabetes and obesity. Bihar, like other parts of north and central India, struggles with malnourishment.

Ideally, each state would get a health budget and decide locally how best to tackle its own problem. Instead, central schemes are designed in Delhi, for the nearby problem, and miss local needs. {026-R11}
~ Ajay Shah supplied the name for the cure: the subsidiarity principle, which places every problem at the lowest level of government where it can be placed. {026-C14}

quote.text: The needs of the North and the South are so different. But the priorities of the North dictate public policy.

stories.postscript: Varma, mid-story, plugged the hosts’ diabetes episode: “We can conquer diabetes. Yes, we can.”

stories.start: So while there is a lot of admiration and respect for the military
stories.end: which were all covered up in the normal pompous parades and nationalism and militarism
stories.caption: military secrecy and Russia’s failures
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on secrecy as a cover for failure
stories.head: Secrets behind the pomp
body: Secrecy is the fourth question in Ajay Shah’s test of difficulty, and his example was an institution held in high regard: the military. {026-S03}

“While there is a lot of admiration and respect for the military, it is also the case that the military is shrouded in secrecy,” he said. That secrecy, he argued, is likely cover for a lot of state failure.
Once the shooting started in Putin’s war, the world found “mind-blowing failures” inside the Russian military. {#putin} They had been covered up by pompous parades, nationalism and militarism.
~ Where a government activity runs under complete transparency, Shah said, more people notice misbehaviour and malfeasance, and there is more check and balance.
stories.why: A grand spectacle says nothing about whether an institution works. Secrecy removes the scrutiny that exposes malfeasance, so the most opaque parts of the state tend to hide the most failure.

quiz.q: What, in the technical sense, makes something a public good, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: It is non-rival and non-excludable, like clean air, not merely good for the public.

quiz.q: Name the four buckets of market failure that economists green-light for state intervention.
quiz.a: Market power, externalities, asymmetric information and public goods; outside them, freedom stays the default.

quiz.q: Why is a polio drive an easy problem for the state, by Shah’s test?
quiz.a: Many transactions, but no discretion: frontline staff simply follow a manual and give the drops.

quiz.q: What principle places every problem at the lowest level of government that can handle it?
quiz.a: The subsidiarity principle, which Ajay Shah called one of the great ideas in economics.

quiz.q: What did DaVinci Resolve cost in 2010, when it only did colour grading?
quiz.a: Eight hundred thousand dollars, so India had no copy and films went to Hollywood.

quiz.q: According to Amit Varma, what did the Nordic countries become before they became welfare states?
quiz.a: Rich, as model free-market economies, as the writer Johan Norberg describes in detail.
